ops.title: SECURITY: the Swift client writes its hello to an unverified peer — no Authorize equivalent
ops.description:
Found 2026-08-01 by the wire-hardening refuter, immediately after the Go half was fixed.

The Go client now refuses a socket squatter before a single byte crosses: `ClientConfig.Authorize` is
required on the unix-dial path, invoked between dial and the hello write. Measured against a real
same-UID squatter that binds the socket first: a forged drain preamble achieves nothing, a forged
build-mismatch ack achieves nothing, and the squatter reads **0 bytes** — the schema digest never
crosses.

**The Swift client has no equivalent.** `Sources/DaemonKit/SocketClient.swift:722` goes
`connect(path:)` -> `configureNonblocking` -> codec -> writer -> `handshake(...)` with no
verification anywhere in the chain. So every attack the Go client now refuses still works against a
Swift consumer: forge the preamble, forge a build mismatch, harvest the schema digest. Worse,
`ServiceSocketClient.waitReady` (:229-255) loops `while true` "across draining successors until
deadline", so a squatter that forges `ErrDraining` pins a Swift consumer for its whole deadline.

This is not hypothetical surface: the Swift half has two live consumers — fusekit imports it directly
at `exact: "0.20.9"`, and cc-pool links it on host, appex and tests with CI gating Go/Swift pin
equality. See [[fusekit-session-roles-collapse-onto-lane-alone]].

The open design question, which is why this is filed rather than fixed: **can Swift read the peer's
code identity at all?** The Go path uses `LOCAL_PEERCRED` for the floor plus `csops_audittoken`
against the peer's audit token, both bound in `internal/trust` through purego. Swift would need an
equivalent — either its own binding, or an XPC/SecCode route, or the check delegated to a Go helper.
That is a real design decision, not a port.

Until it is answered, the CHANGELOG's unscoped "A client judges the process accepting for it before
it writes a byte" overclaims and must be scoped to the Go client.

ops.text: The Swift client verifies the accepting process before writing any byte, or its docs state plainly that it does not and consumers are told what that costs
